newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ALPINE SKIING-RIEGLER HAUNTS AUSTRIA WITH SCARY RESULTS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-RIEGLER HAUNTS AUSTRIA WITH SCARY RESULTS.

text.p: New Zealand's Claudia Riegler continued to haunt the Austrian ski team on Saturday by collecting her second World Cup slalom win of the season.
With the victory, Riegler kept her 100 per cent record in the slalom discipline this season intact and left the Austrian ski federation second-guessing their decision to let her leave the fold.
Wearing a Santa Claus hat and a wide smile, Riegler wished everyone a Merry Christmas as she stepped onto the podium and then explained that the win was an unexpected gift.

"I didn't think it was possible to win here today," Riegler said, after recording her third career success. "Neither of my runs was perfect, the first run was particularly difficult because it was very bumpy.
"But I have a lot of confidence right now and that helped in the second run."

Riegler, who also won the first slalom of the season a month ago in Park City, Utah, clocked the second best time in both trips down the icy Nationale course, finishing with a combined time of one minute 29.83 seconds.

Sweden's world champion Pernilla Wiberg had held a delicate .23-second advantage over Riegler after the first leg but was unable to conserve her lead and had to settle for second behind the Kiwi for the second consecutive race with a time of 1:30.50.

"It wasn't my type of course and the conditions were very difficult, the snow had strange ice balls in it," said Wiberg as she jumped into a waiting car and left immediately for the final race before the Christmas break, a giant slalom in Morzine on Sunday.
Patricia Chauvet of France was third in 1:30.54 followed by teammate Leila Piccard, who had the fastest second run of 44.62 seconds to move from 13th after the first leg to fourth.

After Riegler, who obtained New Zealand citizenship through her Kiwi mother, registered her first career victory last season in Serre Chevalier, a conciliatory Austrian Ski Federation made overtures to the 20-year-old about returning to the team.
Riegler listened to the offers but says she was content to live in Austria and race for New Zealand.
"I'm very comfortable racing in Europe because I can go home between races," said Riegler, who lives just outside of Salzburg. "I have two homes, one in New Zealand and one here."
Germany's Katja Seizinger, the overall World Cup leader and reigning champion, was suffering from the flu and did not race.

Seizinger however, could at least take some comfort in the fact that Wiberg, the Olympic and world combined champion, didn't pick up another 100 points by winning the combined event that was lost when Friday's downhill was postponed.
That allowed the German to escape the weekend with her lead atop the standings intact although her advantage over the Swede has been reduced to just 32 points.
Seizinger will climb out of her sick bed on Sunday to race in Morzine in effort to keep Wiberg from biting further into her lead.
